pos: n. (hue; appearance to the eye; Hebrew 'ayin, literally eye)
etymology: Latin color. The KJV keeps the older British spelling. The Hebrew word most often rendered colour is 'ayin, eye — the appearance of a thing to the eye rather than an abstract property of it.
biblical_def: Colour in Scripture is how a thing looks, and it is often diagnostic. The priest examining a plague in a garment is given colour as a test: “if the plague have not changed his colour, and the plague be not spread; it is unclean; thou shalt burn it in the fire” (Lev 13:55). The manna is described by it: “And the manna was as coriander seed, and the colour thereof as the colour of bdellium” (Num 11:7). Solomon uses it as a warning: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright” (Pro 23:31). And Ezekiel reaches for it twice in the first vision, where nothing quite fits: “out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” (Eze 1:4), and of the living creatures, “they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass” (Eze 1:7). The Hebrew idiom is exact: what the eye of the beholder reports. Ezekiel does not say the wheels were amber. He says what they were like to look at, and stops there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines colour as the appearance of bodies to the eye, or that property which is perceived by the organ of sight; also, appearance to the mind; pretence, false show.
webster_full: COLOR, n. In physics, a property inherent in light, which by a difference in the rays and the laws of refraction produces different sensations.
2. Appearance of a body to the eye; hue; dye.
3. Appearance to the mind; false show; pretence; as, under color of law.
4. In the plural, a flag, ensign or standard.
scriptures: And the priest shall look on the plague, after that it is washed: and, behold, if the plague have not changed his colour, and the plague be not spread; it is unclean; thou shalt burn it in the fire; it is fret inward, whether it be bare within or without.
Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright.
Eze 1:4

And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire.
Eze 1:7
And their feet were straight feet; and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf's foot: and they sparkled like the colour of burnished brass.
corruption_summary: Appearance is trusted as the measure of a thing, while Proverbs points at wine at its most beautiful and says do not look, and Ezekiel refuses to say more than what a thing resembled.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 23:31 is one of the few places Scripture commands a man not to look at something beautiful. The verse describes the wine at its most attractive — red, catching the light, moving in the cup — and forbids the gaze rather than merely the drink, because the appetite is engaged by the eye before the mouth. The next verse names the end: at the last it biteth like a serpent. Temptation in Scripture is rarely ugly, and the counsel is rarely to look harder and reason better; it is to look away.

Ezekiel 1 shows the honest use of the word. Confronted with a vision of the glory, the prophet piles up comparisons — as the colour of amber, like the colour of burnished brass, the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD — and never once claims to describe the thing itself. That reticence is a doctrine. God is not less than what Ezekiel saw; He is more, and the prophet's hedged language is reverence, not vagueness.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ayin (H5869), eye, and so appearance or colour; mar'eh (H4758), appearance, sight; tseva' (H6648), dyed stuff.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ayin (H5869) — eye, appearance, colour; Numbers 11:7, Ezekiel 1:4.
Hebrew mar'eh (H4758) — appearance, vision; Ezekiel's repeated hedge.
Hebrew tsava' (H6648) — dyed garments, colours; Judges 5:30.
Hebrew chashmal (H2830) — amber; the colour out of the midst of the fire.
Hebrew nega' (H5061) — plague, stroke; the thing whose colour the priest examined.
usage: “If the plague have not changed his colour” — appearance as diagnosis.
“Look not thou upon the wine… when it giveth his colour in the cup” — look away.
“As the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” — a likeness, not a description.

etymology: Old English panne. In Leviticus it names one of the appointed ways a meat offering could be prepared; in Samuel it appears in the account of how the priesthood was corrupted.
biblical_def: The pan belongs first to the law of the meat offering, which the LORD permitted to be prepared three ways: in the oven, in the frying pan, or in a pan. “And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in a pan, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mingled with oil” (Lev 2:5). The high priest's own daily offering used it: “In a pan it shall be made with oil; and when it is baken, thou shalt bring it in: and the baken pieces of the meat offering shalt thou offer for a sweet savour unto the LORD” (Lev 6:21). The portions were assigned: “And all the meat offering that is baken in the oven, and all that is dressed in the fryingpan, and in the pan, shall be the priest's that offereth it” (Lev 7:9). Then the word appears in the indictment of Eli's sons: “And he struck it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot; all that the fleshhook brought up the priest took for himself. So they did in Shiloh unto all the Israelites that came thither” (1Sa 2:14). A pan also carries Tamar's cakes into Amnon's chamber (2Sa 13:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pan as a vessel broad and shallow, used for domestic purposes; and notes its Scriptural use for vessels of the sanctuary.
webster_full: PAN, n. A vessel broad and somewhat hollow or depressed in the middle, or with a raised border; used for domestic purposes.
2. The part of a fire-lock which holds the priming.
3. Something hollow; as the brain-pan.
FRYING-PAN, n. A pan with a long handle, used for frying meat and vegetables.
scriptures: Lev 2:5
And if thy oblation be a meat offering baken in a pan, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mingled with oil.
Lev 6:21
In a pan it shall be made with oil; and when it is baken, thou shalt bring it in: and the baken pieces of the meat offering shalt thou offer for a sweet savour unto the LORD.
Lev 7:9
And all the meat offering that is baken in the oven, and all that is dressed in the fryingpan, and in the pan, shall be the priest's that offereth it.
And he struck it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot; all that the fleshhook brought up the priest took for himself. So they did in Shiloh unto all the Israelites that came thither.
corruption_summary: Ministry is treated as a career with entitlements, while 1 Samuel 2 records priests reaching into the pan with a fleshhook and taking what the law had not assigned them.
corruption_paragraphs: The law had already provided generously for the priests: the meat offering baken in the pan was theirs, by God's own appointment. Hophni and Phinehas were not underpaid; they were unsatisfied. So a servant came with a three-pronged fleshhook and struck it into the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot, and whatever came up the priest took — and worse, they demanded raw flesh before the fat was burnt to the LORD. The sin was not greed in the abstract. It was taking by force what God had not assigned, from an offering that belonged to Him first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture regulates even the cooking of an offering. Fine flour, unleavened, mingled with oil, baken in a pan — the LORD specifies the utensil. Where He has provided a form and a portion, the man who improvises is not being spontaneous; and 1 Samuel says that men abhorred the offering of the LORD because of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew machabath (H4227), a flat plate or pan for baking; parur (H6517), a pot or pan; mazleg (H4207), the fleshhook of 1 Samuel 2:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew machabath (H4227) — pan, baking plate; Leviticus 2:5, 6:21, 7:9.
Hebrew parur (H6517) — pan, pot; 1 Samuel 2:14.
Hebrew minchah (H4503) — meat offering, gift; what the pan prepared.
Hebrew mazleg (H4207) — fleshhook; the instrument of the theft at Shiloh.
Hebrew solet (H5560) — fine flour; the specified material.
usage: “A meat offering baken in a pan… of fine flour unleavened, mingled with oil” — the form given.
“Shall be the priest's that offereth it” — the portion assigned.
“He struck it into the pan… all that the fleshhook brought up the priest took for himself” — the portion seized.

pos: n. (the fittings and vessels belonging to a thing; Hebrew keli)
etymology: Old French fourniture, from fournir, to furnish or equip. In the KJV it means the whole set of vessels and implements that belong to a piece of furniture, not the furniture itself.
biblical_def: Furniture in the KJV is the equipment belonging to a thing. The LORD lists the sanctuary's by name when He commissions Bezaleel: “The tabernacle of the congregation, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is thereupon, and all the furniture of the tabernacle” (Exo 31:7); “And the table and his furniture, and the pure candlestick with all his furniture, and the altar of incense” (Exo 31:8); “And the altar of burnt offering with all his furniture, and the laver and his foot” (Exo 31:9). The record of the making repeats it: “The candlestick also for the light, and his furniture, and his lamps, with the oil for the light” (Exo 35:14). The word's other appearance is domestic and disreputable: Rachel, fleeing Laban with her father's household gods, “had taken the images, and put them in the camel's furniture, and sat upon them. And Laban searched all the tent, but found them not” (Gen 31:34). The saddlebags of a camel and the vessels of the tabernacle answer to the same Hebrew word, keli — whatever equips a thing for its use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines furniture as goods, vessels, utensils and other appendages necessary or convenient for a house; also, equipage, ornaments and appendages of any kind.
webster_full: FURNITURE, n. Goods, vessels, utensils and other appendages necessary or convenient for housekeeping.
2. Appendages; that which is added for use or ornament; as the furniture of a saddle.
3. Equipage; ornaments; decorations.
FURNISH, v.t. To supply with any thing necessary, useful or convenient.
scriptures: Exo 31:7
The tabernacle of the congregation, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is thereupon, and all the furniture of the tabernacle,
Exo 31:8
And the table and his furniture, and the pure candlestick with all his furniture, and the altar of incense,
Exo 31:9
And the altar of burnt offering with all his furniture, and the laver and his foot,
Now Rachel had taken the images, and put them in the camel's furniture, and sat upon them. And Laban searched all the tent, but found them not.
corruption_summary: The details of the sanctuary are treated as ceremonial clutter, while the LORD names every vessel He intends and Hebrews calls the whole a pattern of heavenly things.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD itemizes. Exodus 31 could have said make the tabernacle, and instead names the ark, the mercy seat, the table and his furniture, the candlestick with all his furniture, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all his furniture, the laver and his foot. Hebrews 8:5 then says Moses was admonished to make all things according to the pattern shewed him in the mount. An itemized commandment implies an itemized original.

Genesis 31:34 supplies the sharp contrast. The same word covers the fittings of the LORD's dwelling and a camel's saddlebags, and Rachel hid stolen idols in the latter and sat on them. She had left her father's house for the covenant family and brought his gods with her in the luggage. Households leaving one allegiance for another have been doing it ever since, and Jacob had to bury the strange gods under the oak at Shechem before he could go up to Bethel.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (H3627), vessel, implement, equipment — a wide word covering armour, tools, sanctuary vessels and baggage; kar (H3733), the camel's saddle-basket of Genesis 31:34.
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — vessel, furniture, instrument; Exodus 31:7–9, 35:14.
Hebrew kar (H3733) — camel's furniture, a saddle-basket; Genesis 31:34.
Hebrew menorah (H4501) — candlestick; with all his furniture.
Hebrew teraphim (H8655) — images; what Rachel hid in the camel's furniture.
Greek tupos (G5179) — pattern; Hebrews 8:5, the pattern shewed in the mount.
usage: “And the table and his furniture, and the pure candlestick with all his furniture” — itemized.
“The altar of burnt offering with all his furniture, and the laver and his foot” — down to the stand.
“Put them in the camel's furniture, and sat upon them” — idols in the baggage.

pos: v. (shut in; set within a border; Hebrew musabboth, naqaph)
etymology: Latin includere, to shut in. The KJV spelling drops the e. Scripture uses it for stones set in gold, for an army surrounded, and for a man hemmed in by enemies.
biblical_def: Inclosed means shut within a border, and Scripture uses it for the beautiful and the terrible alike. The high priest's stones: “And they wrought onyx stones inclosed in ouches of gold, graven, as signets are graven, with the names of the children of Israel” (Exo 39:6), and of the breastplate's fourth row, “a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper: they were inclosed in ouches of gold in their inclosings” (Exo 39:13). A tribe surrounded in battle: “Thus they inclosed the Benjamites round about, and chased them, and trode them down with ease” (Jdg 20:43). A heart shut up in its own prosperity: “They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly” (Psa 17:10). And the crucifixion psalm, a thousand years before the event: “For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet” (Psa 22:16). The tribal names were inclosed in gold and borne into the holy place; the Son of David was inclosed by the wicked and pierced.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inclose as to surround; to shut in; to encompass; to fence in; to separate from common grounds by a fence; to put within a case or wrapper.
webster_full: INCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut in; to confine on all sides.
2. To separate from common grounds by a fence; as, to inclose land.
3. To include; to shut or confine; as, to inclose a letter in a cover.
INCLOSED, pp. Surrounded; encompassed; confined on all sides; committed within a cover.
scriptures: Exo 39:6
And they wrought onyx stones inclosed in ouches of gold, graven, as signets are graven, with the names of the children of Israel.
Thus they inclosed the Benjamites round about, and chased them, and trode them down with ease over against Gibeah toward the sunrising.
They are inclosed in their own fat: with their mouth they speak proudly.
For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
corruption_summary: Psalm 22 is explained as a poet's general lament, while its details — the piercing, the parted garments, the mockery — match one execution and no other.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 22:16 is among the most contested verses in the Old Testament, and the reason is obvious: they pierced my hands and my feet, written centuries before crucifixion was practised by anyone in that world. Attempts to dissolve it into a general lament have to account for the psalm's other particulars — the parting of the garments and the casting of lots for the vesture, the mockery in the very words the chief priests used, the bones out of joint, and the cry with which the Lord Jesus opened His last hour from the cross. The New Testament writers did not read this psalm as a coincidence, and neither did He.

Psalm 17:10 supplies the other kind of inclosure, and it is the one most Christians in a comfortable country are in danger of. They are inclosed in their own fat — shut in by prosperity, insulated from need, and consequently speaking proudly. Nothing external is holding them; the wall is their own abundance. Scripture treats that condition as more dangerous than the siege at Gibeah, because the man inside it does not know he is surrounded.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqaph (H5362), to surround, encircle; musabboth (H4142), set or inclosed, of stones in settings; ka'ari / karu in Psalm 22:16, they pierced.
roots_lines: Hebrew musabboth (H4142) — inclosed, set about; Exodus 39:6, 39:13.
Hebrew naqaph (H5362) — to surround, compass; Judges 20:43, Psalm 17:9.
Hebrew mishbetsah (H4865) — ouches, settings of gold; what the stones were inclosed in.
Hebrew karah — to dig or pierce; Psalm 22:16, they pierced my hands and my feet.
Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — fat; Psalm 17:10, inclosed in their own fat.
usage: “Onyx stones inclosed in ouches of gold” — names set in gold, borne inward.
“They are inclosed in their own fat” — a wall of one's own abundance.
“The assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet” — written first.

pos: adj. (of or belonging to a servant; laborious; Hebrew 'abodah, work of a bondman)
etymology: Latin servilis, of a slave, from servus. In Leviticus 23 it defines what may not be done on a holy convocation: servile work, the labour of a bondservant.
biblical_def: Servile occurs in the KJV almost entirely in one formula, and that formula structures Israel's calendar. Of unleavened bread: “In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein” (Lev 23:7), and of the seventh day of the feast, “in the seventh day is an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein” (Lev 23:8). Of the feast of weeks: “And ye shall proclaim on the selfsame day, that it may be an holy convocation unto you: ye shall do no servile work therein: it shall be a statute for ever in all your dwellings throughout your generations” (Lev 23:21). Of the feast of trumpets: “Ye shall do no servile work therein: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD” (Lev 23:25). And of tabernacles: “On the first day shall be an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein” (Lev 23:35). The phrase is not a general ban on effort — the same days require offerings, and the priests worked hardest of all. It forbids the labour of a bondman, the work a slave does because he must.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines servile as pertaining to a servant or slave; slavish; dependent; and, of labour, mean, base, or such as is performed by servants.
webster_full: SERVILE, a. Pertaining to a servant or slave; slavish; mean.
2. Dependent; held in subjection; not free.
3. Cringing; fawning; meanly submissive.
SERVITUDE, n. The condition of a slave; the state of involuntary subjection to a master.
scriptures: Lev 23:7
In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein.

And ye shall proclaim on the selfsame day, that it may be an holy convocation unto you: ye shall do no servile work therein: it shall be a statute for ever in all your dwellings throughout your generations.
Ye shall do no servile work therein: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD.
On the first day shall be an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein.
corruption_summary: Rest is treated as recovery time for more production, while Leviticus forbids the labour of a bondman on the LORD's days and commands worship in its place.
corruption_paragraphs: The precision of the phrase is the point. Leviticus does not say do no work on these days; it says do no servile work, the labour of a bondservant. The same chapters command offerings made by fire, which is real labour, and the priests were busiest on the holy convocations. What is forbidden is the work a man does under compulsion, for his living, as a slave does — and the reason is stated in Deuteronomy 5:15: remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt.

This is the standing correction to a productivity culture that has learned to justify rest only as an input to more output. Israel's calendar interrupted the harvest itself; the feast of weeks fell in the middle of the grain, and the LORD required them to stop and assemble. A day off taken to be a better worker on Monday is not what Leviticus commands. The convocation is the point, and the ceasing is what makes room for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mele'keth 'abodah, work of service or servile work; from 'abodah (H5656), labour, bondage — the same root as 'ebed, servant; miqra' qodesh, holy convocation.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abodah (H5656) — service, labour, bondage; the servile work forbidden.
Hebrew 'ebed (H5650) — servant, bondman; the same root, and Israel's memory of Egypt.
Hebrew mela'kah (H4399) — work, occupation; paired with 'abodah in the formula.
Hebrew miqra' qodesh — holy convocation; the positive command of the same verses.
Hebrew shabbathon (H7677) — a sabbath of rest; the character of the day.
usage: “Ye shall do no servile work therein” — five times in one chapter.
“But ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD” — ceasing is not idleness.
“A statute for ever in all your dwellings throughout your generations” — not a seasonal favour.

pos: n. (the east; the quarter where the sun comes up; Hebrew mizrach hashshemesh)
etymology: A KJV compound rendering the Hebrew phrase toward the rising of the sun. Israel oriented itself by sunrise, and the tabernacle's gate faced it.
biblical_def: Sunrising is the KJV's way of naming the east by the thing that marks it. Israel's wilderness march is charted by it: “And they journeyed from Oboth, and pitched at Ijeabarim, in the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising” (Num 21:11). So is the trans-Jordan inheritance: “The two tribes and the half tribe have received their inheritance on this side Jordan near Jericho eastward, toward the sunrising” (Num 34:15). Moses fixes the cities of refuge by it: “Then Moses severed three cities on this side Jordan toward the sunrising” (Deu 4:41), and describes the conquered land the same way, “the land of Og king of Bashan, two kings of the Amorites, which were on this side Jordan toward the sunrising” (Deu 4:47). The east is where the tabernacle's one gate opened, where Eden's cherubim stood guard, where Ezekiel saw the glory return, and where the Lord Jesus said His coming would be as the lightning that shineth from the east even unto the west.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sunrising as the first appearance of the sun above the horizon; the time of such appearance; and the east.
webster_full: SUN-RISING, n. The first appearance of the sun above the horizon in the morning; also, the time of such appearance.
2. The east.
EAST, n. The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to rise at the equinox, or the corresponding point on the earth.
scriptures: And they journeyed from Oboth, and pitched at Ijeabarim, in the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising.
The two tribes and the half tribe have received their inheritance on this side Jordan near Jericho eastward, toward the sunrising.
Deu 4:41
Then Moses severed three cities on this side Jordan toward the sunrising;
Deu 4:47
And they possessed his land, and the land of Og king of Bashan, two kings of the Amorites, which were on this side Jordan toward the sunrising;
corruption_summary: Direction in Scripture is read as incidental geography, while the east is consistently the quarter of entrance, exile and return.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's compass carries meaning. Man was driven out of Eden eastward and the cherubim were placed at the east of the garden; the tabernacle and the temple opened to the east; the glory departed by the east gate in Ezekiel 10 and returned by it in Ezekiel 43; and the wise men came from the east having seen a star. A reader who treats toward the sunrising as filler is skipping a thread the prophets deliberately picked up.

Deuteronomy 4:41 is worth noticing in its own right. Moses, forbidden to enter the land, spent part of his last strength severing three cities of refuge on the side of Jordan he could reach — toward the sunrising — so that a man who killed his neighbour unawares would have somewhere to run. He legislated mercy for a country he would never see. That is the character of the office, and Hebrews says the same of the patriarchs, who died in faith, not having received the promises.
roots_summary: Hebrew mizrach (H4217), the place of rising, the east; from zarach (H2224), to rise or shine forth — the verb of Malachi 4:2, the Sun of righteousness shall arise.
roots_lines: Hebrew mizrach (H4217) — east, sunrising; Numbers 21:11, 34:15, Deuteronomy 4:41.
Hebrew zarach (H2224) — to rise, to shine forth; Malachi 4:2.
Hebrew shemesh (H8121) — sun; the second element of the Hebrew phrase.
Hebrew qedem (H6924) — east, also ancient time; the other Hebrew word for the quarter.
Greek anatole (G395) — the dayspring, the rising; Luke 1:78, the dayspring from on high.
usage: “In the wilderness which is before Moab, toward the sunrising” — the march, charted by dawn.
“Then Moses severed three cities… toward the sunrising” — refuge, on the side he could reach.
The east is the quarter of the gate, the exile, and the return.

pos: n. (a tent, especially a royal or divine one; Hebrew sukkah, shaphrur)
etymology: Old French pavillon, from Latin papilio, a butterfly — a tent whose spread canvas resembles wings. Scripture uses it of a king's field tent and of God's own hiding place.
biblical_def: A pavilion is a tent, and in the Psalms it is God's. David describes the LORD coming down in storm: “He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies” (Psa 18:11). Then he turns the same word into refuge: “For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock” (Psa 27:5). And again, with a threat named that no rock protects against: “Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues” (Psa 31:20). The word's other use is imperial: the LORD tells Jeremiah that Nebuchadrezzar “shall spread his royal pavilion” over stones hidden at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Egypt (Jer 43:10). Two pavilions, then — the one a conqueror pitches over a country he has taken, and the one God pitches over a man in trouble.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pavilion as a tent; a temporary movable habitation; and in Scripture, a covering or place of shelter.
webster_full: PAVILION, n. A tent; a temporary movable habitation.
2. In architecture, a kind of turret or building, usually insulated and contained under a single roof.
3. In heraldry, a covering in form of a tent, investing the armories of kings.
PAVILION, v.t. To furnish with tents; to shelter with a tent.
scriptures: He made darkness his secret place; his pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds of the skies.
Psa 27:5
For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock.
Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man: thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues.

And say unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will send and take Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will set his throne upon these stones that I have hid; and he shall spread his royal pavilion over them.
corruption_summary: The refuge God offers is imagined as removal from trouble, while the Psalms place the pavilion in the time of trouble and name the strife of tongues as one of the things it shelters from.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 27:5 is careful about timing: in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion. Not before it and not instead of it. The shelter is inside the season, which is why the same psalm can say, though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Prayer that treats God's protection as the removal of the trouble has asked for something David did not ask for and did not receive.

Psalm 31:20 names a peril that most theologies of protection overlook: the strife of tongues. Slander, gossip, the organized contempt of men — a rock does not help against these, and neither does strength. David says the LORD keeps His people secretly in a pavilion from it, in the secret of His presence. A man whose name is being destroyed has somewhere to be, and Psalm 18 tells us what that place looks like from outside: darkness, dark waters, thick clouds. God's hiding places are not transparent to the people looking for you.
roots_summary: Hebrew sukkah (H5521), booth, pavilion — the same word as the booths of Tabernacles; shaphrur (H8237), a royal canopy, in Jeremiah 43:10; sether (H5643), secret place.
roots_lines: Hebrew sukkah (H5521) — pavilion, booth; Psalm 18:11, 31:20, and the feast of tabernacles.
Hebrew shaphrur (H8237) — royal pavilion; Jeremiah 43:10, used once.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — secret place, covert; paired with the pavilion in Psalm 27:5.
Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, treasure up; he shall hide me in his pavilion.
Hebrew rib leshonoth — the strife of tongues; Psalm 31:20.
usage: “In the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion” — inside the season, not instead of it.
“From the strife of tongues” — a peril no rock answers.
“His pavilion round about him were dark waters and thick clouds” — the shelter looks like storm from outside.

pos: n. (an aromatic bark; a spice of the holy oil; Hebrew qinnamon, Greek kinnamomon)
etymology: Hebrew qinnamon, passing into Greek and Latin nearly unchanged — one of the oldest trade words in the languages of the Mediterranean, carried west with the spice itself.
biblical_def: Cinnamon appears four times in Scripture, and the four are a moral map. It is an ingredient of the holy anointing oil, which no man might compound for himself: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels” (Exo 30:23). It is in the mouth of the strange woman, inviting a young man to a bed she has prepared: “I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon” (Pro 7:17). It is in the garden of the bride, among the chief spices of a love that is lawful: “Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices” (Son 4:14). And it is in the cargo manifest of Babylon the great, in a list that begins with luxuries and ends with people: “And cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men” (Rev 18:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cinnamon as the bark of a tree, a species of laurus, of a fragrant smell and pungent taste, brought from Ceylon and used as a spice.
webster_full: CINNAMON, n. The bark of a species of laurus or bay tree, a native of Ceylon.
2. The tree which produces the cinnamon of commerce.
SPICE, n. A vegetable production, fragrant or aromatic to the smell and pungent to the taste, used in sauces and in cookery.
scriptures: Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,
Pro 7:17
I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.
Son 4:14
Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:
And cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men.
corruption_summary: Pleasure is judged by its intensity rather than by its setting, while the same spice marks the holy oil, the harlot's bed, the bride's garden and the merchandise of Babylon.
corruption_paragraphs: One substance, four settings, and the settings decide everything. Cinnamon in the anointing oil is holy, and Exodus 30 warns that whoever compounds any like it shall be cut off from his people. Cinnamon on the strange woman's bed in Proverbs 7 is the bait of a trap that leads down to the chambers of death. Cinnamon in the Song of Solomon is the fragrance of a garden enclosed, a spring shut up, a fountain sealed — the same delight, inside a covenant. The thing is not the question. Where it is offered, and by whom, and under what promise, is the question.

Revelation 18:13 draws the line under it. John lists the cargo Babylon can no longer sell — cinnamon near the top, and slaves and souls of men at the bottom, in the same breath and the same sentence. That is the commercial system's own valuation, and Scripture reproduces it without comment because none is needed. An economy that will trade in spice and in people has already told you what it thinks a person is worth.
roots_summary: Hebrew qinnamon (H7076), cinnamon; Greek kinnamomon (G2792); the compound of Exodus 30 also uses mor, myrrh, and qaneh, calamus.
roots_lines: Hebrew qinnamon (H7076) — cinnamon; Exodus 30:23, Proverbs 7:17, Song of Solomon 4:14.
Greek kinnamomon (G2792) — cinnamon; Revelation 18:13.
Hebrew mor (H4753) — myrrh; named beside it in all three Hebrew passages.
Hebrew shemen mishchath qodesh — holy anointing oil; the compound cinnamon belonged to.
Greek gomos (G1117) — merchandise, cargo; the list in Revelation 18.
usage: “Of sweet cinnamon half so much” — measured out for the holy oil.
“I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon” — the same spice, baiting a trap.
“And cinnamon… and slaves, and souls of men” — one manifest, top and bottom.

pos: n. (splendid display; the parade of greatness; Hebrew ga'on, hamon)
etymology: Greek pompe, a solemn procession, through Latin. Every occurrence in the KJV is in a prophecy of that pomp being brought down.
biblical_def: Pomp in Scripture is always on its way to the grave. Isaiah watches it swallowed: “Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it” (Isa 5:14). In the taunt over the king of Babylon he addresses it directly: “Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee” (Isa 14:11). Ezekiel announces the same of Jerusalem's strong men: “I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled” (Eze 7:24). And twice of Egypt: “the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity” (Eze 30:18), and “they shall spoil the pomp of Egypt, and all the multitude thereof shall be destroyed” (Eze 32:12). The word never once describes something that lasts. Its whole biblical career is a series of announcements that it is ending.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pomp as a procession distinguished by ostentation of grandeur; splendor; parade; and, in general, ostentatious display of greatness.
webster_full: POMP, n. A procession distinguished by ostentation of grandeur and splendor; as the pomp of a Roman triumph.
2. Show of magnificence; parade; splendor.
POMPOUS, a. Displaying pomp; showy with grandeur; splendid; magnificent.
2. Ostentatious; boastful; as a pompous account of private adventures.
scriptures: Isa 5:14
Therefore hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure: and their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp, and he that rejoiceth, shall descend into it.
Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee.
Eze 7:24
Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled.

At Tehaphnehes also the day shall be darkened, when I shall break there the yokes of Egypt: and the pomp of her strength shall cease in her: as for her, a cloud shall cover her, and her daughters shall go into captivity.
corruption_summary: Grandeur is taken as evidence of permanence, while every occurrence of the word in Scripture stands inside a sentence announcing its end.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 14:11 is one of the most deliberately humiliating verses in the prophets, and the technique is juxtaposition. Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee. The music and the maggots in one sentence. The prophet does not argue that splendour is wicked; he simply reports where it ends, and lets the reader do the arithmetic. That is the pattern of the whole word in Scripture — not denunciation, but a shortened time horizon.

Ezekiel 7:24 names the cost precisely: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled. The pomp of the strong and the holy places fall together, because a religion that has become an apparatus of national dignity has nothing left when the dignity goes. The church that builds its credibility on cultural standing is buying its own obituary in advance, and the prophets have already written it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ga'on (H1347), excellency, pride, pomp; hamon (H1995), multitude, tumult — the roar of a crowd; she'on (H7588), noise or pomp, in Isaiah 5:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew she'on (H7588) — pomp, tumult, roar; Isaiah 5:14.
Hebrew ga'on (H1347) — excellency, pomp, pride; Ezekiel 7:24, 30:18, 32:12.
Hebrew hamon (H1995) — multitude, noise; paired with pomp in the same verses.
Hebrew she'ol (H7585) — hell, the grave; what enlarged herself in Isaiah 5:14.
Hebrew rimmah (H7415) — worm, maggot; Isaiah 14:11, spread under the king of Babylon.
usage: “Their glory, and their multitude, and their pomp… shall descend into it” — all three together.
“Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols” — music and maggots, one verse.
“I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease” — and the holy places fell with it.

etymology: Old French javelin, a light spear for casting. In the KJV it belongs to two men: a priest who used one in zeal, and a king who threw one in envy.
biblical_def: The javelin appears in Scripture in two hands, and the contrast is the entry. Phinehas took one when Israel was joined to Baalpeor and a man brought a Midianitish woman into the camp in the sight of Moses and the weeping congregation: “And when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, and took a javelin in his hand” (Num 25:7) — and the plague was stayed, and God gave him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Saul took one at home, with music playing: “there was a javelin in Saul's hand” (1Sa 18:10). “And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice” (1Sa 18:11). He tried again: “And Saul sought to smite David even to the wall with the javelin; but he slipped away out of Saul's presence, and he smote the javelin into the wall: and David fled, and escaped that night” (1Sa 19:10). One man threw a weapon at open covenant treachery and stopped a plague. The other threw one at a musician who was serving him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a javelin as a sort of spear about five feet and a half long, the shaft of which was of wood, with a steel point; used by horse and foot.
webster_full: JAVELIN, n. A sort of spear about five feet and a half long, the shaft of which was of wood, with a steel point.
SPEAR, n. A long pointed weapon, used in war and hunting, by thrusting or throwing.
ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, ardor in the pursuit of good.
scriptures: Num 25:7
And when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw it, he rose up from among the congregation, and took a javelin in his hand;

And it came to pass on the morrow, that the evil spirit from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of the house: and David played with his hand, as at other times: and there was a javelin in Saul's hand.
And Saul cast the javelin; for he said, I will smite David even to the wall with it. And David avoided out of his presence twice.
And Saul sought to smite David even to the wall with the javelin; but he slipped away out of Saul's presence, and he smote the javelin into the wall: and David fled, and escaped that night.
corruption_summary: Zeal is either despised as fanaticism or claimed as cover for private malice, while Scripture sets Phinehas and Saul side by side and judges them by what they were defending.
corruption_paragraphs: Phinehas is the hardest case in Scripture for a modern conscience, and the text does not soften it. Israel was in open covenant apostasy, a plague was killing thousands, a prince of Simeon paraded his sin before the door of the tabernacle while the congregation wept, and a priest acted. The LORD's own verdict is recorded: he was zealous for my sake among them, and the plague was stayed. Psalm 106 says it was counted unto him for righteousness. Whatever else this is, it is not a private man avenging a private grievance; it is the appointed guardian of the sanctuary defending the sanctuary.

Saul is the counterfeit, and the counterfeit is instructive. He also had a weapon in his hand, he also acted suddenly, and he also could have called it zeal for the kingdom. But the evil spirit was upon him, the provocation was a song the women had sung, and the target was the man playing the harp for him. The difference between Phinehas and Saul is not temperament or even violence; it is whose honour was at stake. Jealousy for God stopped a plague. Jealousy for self spent the rest of a reign chasing a shepherd through caves.
roots_summary: Hebrew romach (H7420), a lance or javelin, in Numbers 25:7; chanith (H2595), spear or javelin, in Saul's hand; qin'ah (H7068), zeal or jealousy — the word used of both men.
roots_lines: Hebrew romach (H7420) — javelin, lance; Numbers 25:7, of Phinehas.
Hebrew chanith (H2595) — spear, javelin; 1 Samuel 18:10, 19:10, of Saul.
Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — zeal, jealousy; the covenant of peace given for it, Numbers 25:11.
Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — plague; stayed at twenty and four thousand.
Hebrew berith shalom — covenant of peace; what Phinehas received.
usage: “Phinehas… rose up from among the congregation, and took a javelin in his hand” — and the plague was stayed.
“And Saul cast the javelin” — at the man playing his harp.
“He smote the javelin into the wall” — and David escaped that night.
